Follow these writing rules. They matter as much as the content:

- Bold used as body emphasis throughout -- reserve bold for a rare callout
- A short rhetorical question with a canned answer -- collapse into one direct statement
- Short buildup, then a reveal: "The best part: it learns." -- state it as a plain sentence
- Emoji or decorative checkmarks in body text -- cut them
- An em dash, section sign or middle dot written as an HTML entity -- write the plain character
- Throat-clearing openers: "needless to say", "at the end of the day" -- state the point directly from the first sentence
- Fake ID tags opening list items: "R-1.", "US-01" -- number the list plainly
- Marketing adjectives: seamless, robust, cutting-edge -- say what is actually true
- The "not just X but Y" construction -- make the point once
- Body paragraphs nearly identical in length -- vary them with what each paragraph has to do
- A significance clause bolted to a sentence: ", underscoring the..." -- delete it, or make it a claim with something behind it
- Three parallel -ing items in a series -- keep the one that carries information
- Fake-humility feedback requests: "would love your feedback on this" -- cut them
- Horizontal rules dropped between sections -- headings already separate sections
- Headings Capitalised Like This -- sentence case
- Vague intensifiers with no number behind them: very, really, quite, significantly -- say how much, or cut the word
- Unnamed authority: "studies show", "experts agree" -- name the actual source, or cut the claim

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write the charter for a newly formed platform engineering team. Around 250 words.

# Charter: platform engineering

## Why we exist

Product teams at this company spend roughly a third of their engineering hours on work that has nothing to do with their product: wiring CI, chasing flaky deploys, re-deriving the same Terraform for the fourth time. We take that work off them and run it once, well.

## What we own

We own the paved road from a commit to production traffic: build pipelines, deployment tooling, the Kubernetes clusters underneath, secrets distribution, and the base observability stack. We own the golden-path templates for new services in Go and TypeScript. We own the on-call rotation for everything in that list.

We do not own product code, product SLOs, or product on-call. When a service pages at 3am because of a bad query, that page goes to the team who wrote the query.

## How we work

The road is paved, not walled. A team can leave it, and we will help them, but they carry the operational cost of doing so. Anything we require rather than recommend gets written down with the reason attached.

We treat internal users as users. Every quarter we run the developer survey and publish the results unedited, including the parts that make us look bad.

## How we know it is working

Three numbers, reviewed monthly: median time from merge to production, the count of production changes rolled back within an hour, and the share of surveyed engineers who say the platform helped more than it cost them last quarter.

Our first target is a service scaffolded and serving traffic in under one working day.

The text above has these problems. Rewrite it so none remain.
Change nothing else, and keep the same length and purpose.

- colon_reveal (Charter:):
- colon_reveal (Three numbers, reviewed monthly:):
- paragraph_uniformity (6 paragraphs, spread 0.22):

Return only the rewritten text.
